### 2.1 C3 (c3)

`data/benchmarks/language/c3.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-09 · last verified 2026-11-09

*Multiple-choice Chinese reading comprehension on dialogues and mixed-genre texts from Chinese second-language exams.*

A Chinese machine reading comprehension dataset: 19,577 free-form multiple-choice questions on 13,369 documents, collected from real and practice Chinese-as-a-second-language examinations (HSK and MHK). A system reads a document and a question and picks the one correct option of two to four; the score is accuracy. Documents are either dialogues (C3-Dialogue, 9,571 questions) or more formally written mixed-genre texts such as stories, news reports and advertisements (C3-Mixed, 10,006 questions). The authors' annotation of 600 development and test questions found that 86.8% need knowledge beyond the document as well as within it, most often general world knowledge. Train, development and test splits (60/20/20) are all public with their answers, under a non-commercial research-use statement. The paper's best fine-tuned model scored 68.5% on test against a human 96.0% on an annotated subset; 2025 base-model reports score 76.7% to 97.6% depending on protocol. There is no leaderboard of its own; CLUE redistributes it as a task, and OpenCompass runs that copy.

#### c3 · Domain and capabilities

- `domain.secondary` = reasoning-general/commonsense · [S1][c3-s1]
  - why: The authors' annotation of 600 development and test questions found 86.8% need knowledge beyond the document as well as within it, and 57.3% general world knowledge, which the paper calls commonsense knowledge; the commonsense leaf is everyday knowledge not stated in the prompt.
  > It refers to the general knowledge about how the world works, sometimes called commonsense knowledge.
- `domain` = primary language/understanding; secondary reasoning-general/commonsense · [S1][c3-s1]
  - why: Every question comes with the document it is about and the answer is chosen against that document, the understanding leaf's case; the paper frames the task as machine reading comprehension. Its own analysis is that most questions also need knowledge the document does not state, above all general world knowledge, so reasoning-general/commonsense is a secondary.
  > These tasks require a machine reader to answer questions relevant to a given document provided as input
- `capability` = context-integration · [S1][c3-s1]
  - why: The protocol supplies the document that the question is about and scores whether the system picked the option that the document, read with ordinary knowledge, supports.
  > answering 86.8% of questions requires both knowledge within and beyond the accompanying document
- `evaluation_method` = multiple-choice · [S1][c3-s1]
  - why: The system picks one of the supplied options (two to four, 3.8 on average) and accuracy is the score. The chance baseline is the paper's Random row, 27.1% on development and 27.2% on test for C3 as a whole.
  > C3 Dev Test 27.1 27.2 43.8 43.1
- `designed_for_subjects` = task-specific-supervised-model · [S1][c3-s1]
  - why: The dataset has a 60% training split, and the paper's baselines (a rule-based method, Co-Matching and four fine-tuned Chinese BERT variants) are trained on C3's two subsets together and tested on each.
  > We use CM3 and C3D together to train a neural model and perform testing on them separately

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `language/dialogue` · [S1][c3-s1]
  - why: Nearly half the problems are about a dialogue, but the system reads a finished dialogue and answers a question about it; it never conducts one, which is what the dialogue leaf scores.
  > 48.4% of problems require dialogue understanding
- `domain` not `language/long-context` · [S1][c3-s1]
  - why: Documents are short (116.9 characters on average), and the paper itself says the dataset is not suited to lengthy texts.
  > C3 may not be suitable for evaluating the comprehension ability of machine readers on lengthy texts
- `domain` not `general-intelligence/multi-subject-knowledge-exams` · [S1][c3-s1]
  - why: The problems come from exams, but from language-proficiency exams of one subject, Chinese reading comprehension, and every question has its document; the claim is reading comprehension, not breadth of subject knowledge. This is why C3 was taken and C-Eval and CMMLU were not.
  > \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\]

8. (field `domain.secondary`) reasoning-general/commonsense as a secondary rests on the paper's own analysis (57.3% of annotated questions need general world knowledge, which it calls commonsense). The commonsense leaf asks for knowledge not stated anywhere in the prompt, while C3's questions need it together with the document, so a reviewer may prefer no secondary.
9. (field `as_used`) OpenCompass runs CLUE's copy (data/CLUE/C3/dev\_0.json), and the file's relation to C3's development split (both subsets pooled, 3,816 questions, or one subset) was not established; the OpenCompass data package was not downloaded. · [S4][c3-s4]
   > path='./data/CLUE/C3/dev\_0.json'
10. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type academic-lab rests on the author block (Cornell University and Tencent AI Lab), read but not quoted because it carries e-mail addresses; consortium or industry-lab are possible readings. No independence flag was set on the Tencent affiliation.
11. (field `lineage`) The CLUE relationship is recorded as a lineage\_note rather than a fork, since CLUE's C3 task is the same items in another maintainer's suite. If CLUE is catalogued, the lead should decide whether C3 is a member it links to and whether the CLUE test set carries C3's labels or its own hidden copy. · [S11][c3-s11]
   > 数据量：训练集(11,869)，验证集(3,816)，测试集(3,892)

### 2.2 AlignBench (alignbench)

`data/benchmarks/language/alignbench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-09 · last verified 2026-11-09

*683 real-user Chinese queries in eight categories, each answer rated 1-10 by a GPT-4 judge against a revised reference.*

A Chinese benchmark of how well chat assistants serve user requests ("alignment" in the helpfulness sense), from Tsinghua University's Knowledge Engineering Group and Zhipu AI. It holds 683 single-turn queries in eight categories: fundamental language ability, advanced Chinese understanding, open-ended questions, writing, logical reasoning, mathematics, task-oriented role play and professional knowledge. The queries come mainly from real users of the ChatGLM online service, with a minority written by the researchers; half the candidates were discarded as too easy after GPT-3.5-turbo, ChatGLM and Sparkdesk answered them well. Each query has a reference answer that GPT-4 drafted and annotators revised, with web evidence for knowledge-heavy ones. A judge model (gpt-4-0613 in the paper and README) sees the query, the answer and the reference, writes an analysis along category-specific dimensions (correctness, user satisfaction, clarity, creativity and others), scores each and then gives an overall 1-10 rating, with the reference anchored at 8. The headline is the mean of a reasoning score (mathematics and logic) and a language score (the other six categories). Version 1.1 (2024-06-15) keeps the 683 queries and corrects the references of fact-heavy items. The paper measures the judge against human ratings on 400 queries and names position, verbosity and self-enhancement bias as open problems. OpenCompass ships it as a subjective dataset, and model reports such as Qwen3's still cite AlignBench v1.1.

**Evidence** (41 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### alignbench · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][alignbench-s1]
  > We design a human-in-the-loop data curation pipeline, containing eight main categories, 683 real-scenario rooted queries and corresponding human verified references.
- `released` = 2023-11-30 · [S2][alignbench-s2]

#### alignbench · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary language/generation · [S1][alignbench-s1]
  - why: Every item is an open request answered in free-form Chinese text, and the score is a judge's 1-10 rating of that text against a reference answer and category-specific criteria, which is the generation leaf's case ("scored against reference texts or rubric criteria"). The claim is one competence, alignment with user intent in Chinese, not coverage of many subjects.
  > the output is an multi-dimensional analytical explanation and a final rating, ranging from 1 to 10
- `capability` = instruction-following · [S1][alignbench-s1]
  - why: The source counts following human instructions as part of the alignment it measures, and the judge scores "user satisfaction" (满足用户需求) as its own dimension on every answer; writing items carry explicit directions such as formatting conditions.
  > Alignment, including following human instructions and providing helpful assistance
- `evaluation_method` = model-graded-judge · [S1][alignbench-s1]
  - why: A general model prompted with a grading instruction decides each answer's quality, and the reported number is its 1-10 overall ratings averaged.
  > GPT-4 is instructed to generate explanations from multiple dimensions before providing a final grade on a scale of 1 to 10.
- `designed_for_subjects` = instruction-tuned-model · [S1][alignbench-s1]
  - why: The benchmark is built to evaluate instruction-tuned chat assistants on real user requests, prompting the model directly with each query; generation temperature is set per category.
  > we set temperature to 0.1 to ensure more deterministic and reproducible generation

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `language/dialogue` · [S3][alignbench-s3]
  - why: Each item is one user query and one answer; OpenCompass's config sends the question as a single human turn, and nothing is scored across turns.
  > mode='singlescore'
- `domain` not `safety-alignment/harmlessness-refusal` · [S1][alignbench-s1]
  - why: "Alignment" here means fulfilling user intent and preference. Harm enters only as a judging rule (a harmful answer is capped at 1-2) and the queries were desensitised; refusal is not the scored quantity.
  > Desensitization: Ensure that the queries are safe and insensitive.
- `domain` not `language/understanding` · [S1][alignbench-s1]
  - why: Advanced Chinese understanding is one category of 58 queries about Chinese culture and history, and no passage determines the answers.
  > understand cultural and historical background in Chinese-specific tasks
- `capability` not `factual-precision` · [S4][alignbench-s4]
  - why: Correctness (事实正确性) is a judged dimension and dominates the overall score, but the judge rates it as a whole; asserted particulars are not checked one by one against the reference.
  > 其中，事实正确性和满足用户需求这两个维度是最重要的，这两个维度的分数主导了最后的综合分数。
- `capability` not `generation-fidelity` · [S1][alignbench-s1]
  - why: The reference answer is a scoring pivot (it would earn 8), not a target to match; an answer better than the reference scores 9-10.
  > Additionally, we set the reference answer to score 8 as a reference scoring pivot.
- `evaluation_method` not `rubric-graded` · [S4][alignbench-s4]
  - why: The judge scores named dimensions one by one, but the overall rating it issues is its own synthesis (综合每个维度的评估), not a fixed combination of those scores, and the headline averages that overall rating. See review\_checks.
  > \3. 最后，综合每个维度的评估，对AI助手的回答给出一个1～10的综合分数。
- `evaluation_method` not `human-expert-eval` · [S1][alignbench-s1]
  - why: Annotators rated 3,200 answers on a 1-5 scale to validate the judge; scores on the benchmark come from the judge.
  > producing a total of 3200 question-answer pairings
- `evaluation_method` not `pairwise-preference-elo` · [S1][alignbench-s1]
  - why: Grading is point-wise by design; the pairwise comparisons in the paper rate the judges' explanations, not systems.
  > Therefore ALIGNBENCH adopts point-wise grading either.

It fills language/generation, which had no primary entry on main (writingbench, drafted in parallel, also takes it); its data is open on GitHub; its paper is ACL 2024; and it is still reported in 2025 model reports (Qwen3). LCSTS (EMNLP 2015) is filed by OpenCompass under Understanding and would have been a second summarisation set beside xlsum. CompassArena and OpenCompass's other subjective sets were not read, and CLUE, CMRC 2018 and C3 were left to another agent. · [S10][alignbench-s10]

(field `versions`) v1 and v1.1 are revisions (same 683 queries, corrected references), and v1.1 is marked breaking because changed references move the judge's pivot; the sources do not say whether v1 and v1.1 scores are comparable. v1's file is no longer in the repository, and the English README still names it. · [S6][alignbench-s6]
   > The data is placed in \`data/data\_release.jsonl\`
6. (field `evaluation_method`) The judge. The paper and README use gpt-4-0613, shut down on 2026-10-23; CritiqueLLM, the maintainers' own judge, is claimed to recover 95% of GPT-4's evaluation ability; OpenCompass's config does not name a judge, and the Qwen3 report does not say which it used. Published AlignBench numbers are therefore often not comparable, and the reproducibility tier may need the hosted-judge blocker the execution vocabulary deferred. · [S6][alignbench-s6]
   > CritiqueLLM, which could recover 95% of GPT-4's evaluation ability
7. (field `governance.independence_flags`) maintainer-competes-on-own-benchmark rests on the THUDM organisation listing ChatGLM as its project and on ChatGLM models in the paper's table. The paper does not say in words that ChatGLM is the maintainers' model; its authors interned at Zhipu AI and its queries came from "an online LLM service" it leaves anonymous, which the Chinese README names as ChatGLM's. · [S1][alignbench-s1]
   > Based on observations from an online LLM service (anonymous due to review policy)
8. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type academic-lab, following the AgentBench entry in the same THUDM organisation, whose description names Zhipu.ai (Z.ai) and KEG jointly. industry-lab (Zhipu AI) or community-collective (an organisation shared by two institutions with no single stated holder) could be argued. · [S8][alignbench-s8]
   > "description":"ChatGLM, GLM-4, CogVLM, CodeGeeX, CogView, ImageReward, CogVideoX \| CogDL, GraphMAE, AMiner \| Zhipu.ai (Z.ai) & Knowledge Engineering Group (KEG)","name":"THUKEG"
9. (field `activity`) activity no-submission-channel rather than closed. The website's Submit function was a private scoring service and no source shows it publishing outside results; if it fed a public ranking, the lapsed domain would make this closed with a channel-closed history event. · [S6][alignbench-s6]
   > AlignBench \[Website\](https://llmbench.ai/align) is now officially online
10. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk medium with no evidence. No Source states a contamination finding; the queries came from the maintainers' own service's users, which is a route for ChatGLM in particular that no source examines. The paper also says the LLM generations are released, but the repository's data directory now holds only the v1.1 query file (GitHub contents API, not quoted), so records\_access is left unset.
11. (field `capability`) capability instruction-following rests on the paper counting instruction following within alignment and on the user-satisfaction dimension; the overall score does not isolate compliance from quality, as the term's definition would like.

### 2.3 WritingBench (writingbench)

`data/benchmarks/language/writingbench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-09 · last verified 2026-11-09

*1,000 Chinese and English writing tasks in six domains, each graded on five query-specific criteria by an LLM judge.*

A benchmark of 1,000 writing queries (555 English, 445 Chinese) in six domains and 100 subdomains: Academic & Engineering, Finance & Business, Politics & Law, Literature & Arts, Education, and Advertising & Marketing. The Literature & Arts domain (183 queries) holds the creative tasks, such as novel manuscripts and outlines, poetry, screenplays, fan fiction and lyrics. Queries were drafted by GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet, diversified with style, format and length requirements, and then revised by experts, with reference material collected by trained annotators from public documents; inputs run from tens to thousands of words. Each query carries five criteria that Claude-3.7 wrote for it, each with a 1-10 rubric. A judge scores the response against each criterion separately and the score is the mean over criteria and queries; the leaderboard multiplies it by ten. The paper's own table uses a critic model fine-tuned from Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct on 155K Claude-3.7 judgments; the leaderboard has used Claude models as judge, Claude-3-7-Sonnet from April 2025, Claude-Sonnet-4 from September 2025 and Claude-Sonnet-4-5 since 2025-11-27. The first release (March 2025) had 1,239 queries. Separate scores are kept for the style, format and length requirements, the six domains, the 100 subdomains and the two languages.

#### writingbench · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary language/generation; secondary language/creative-writing · [S1][writingbench-s1]
  - why: Every item asks for free-form text that is scored against rubric criteria written for that query, which is the generation leaf's definition. The claim is writing across six domains, most of them functional (papers, reports, contracts, lesson plans, advertising copy); the Literature & Arts domain, novels, poetry, scripts and critiques, is the creative-writing leaf's case, and its subset carries that leaf as primary.
  > Literature & Art: This domain covers the creative and expressive realms of writing, including novels, poetry, scripts, artistic designs, and critiques of books and movies.
- `capability` = context-integration · [S1][writingbench-s1]
  - why: Most queries supply reference material (financial statements, legal templates, manuscripts to continue), and the per-query criteria were introduced so that the judge checks whether a response uses it, such as incorporating data points or keeping narrative continuity.
  > Material dependency: they are insufficient to verify whether responses appropriately utilize the provided reference materials
- `evaluation_method` = rubric-graded, model-graded-judge · [S1][writingbench-s1]
  - why: A rubric of five named criteria is applied per query, each criterion scored on its own by a judge model with a justification, and the scores are averaged.
  > Each query is assessed by 5 instance-specific criteria using a 10-point scale scoring by our critic model.
- `designed_for_subjects` = instruction-tuned-model · [S1][writingbench-s1]
  - why: The queries are written as requests to an assistant, answered in one response with no tools or loop; the leaderboard's rows are chat and reasoning models.
  > initial writing query drafts that simulate realistic user requests

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `language/long-context` · [S1][writingbench-s1]
  - why: Inputs reach 19,361 tokens, but the difficulty is not designed to come from length; length is one of several properties the queries vary, and the score is writing quality.
  > WritingBench supports extended-context generation with input ranging from tens to thousands of words
- `capability` not `instruction-following` · [S1][writingbench-s1]
  - why: Queries carry style, format and length requirements, scored in their own subsets, but the source calls them writing requirements and grades them by degree on 1-10 rubrics inside the quality score; it does not claim instruction following, which the term's inclusion test requires.
  > For each requirement, we create two evaluation subsets.
- `evaluation_method` not `model-derived-metric` · [S1][writingbench-s1]
  - why: The critic is a released fine-tuned checkpoint, but it issues a 1-10 grade and a justification against a criterion written for each query, not a fixed label set, and the leaderboard's judge is a general model prompted to grade.
  > The critic model is fine-tuned on a dataset of 155K instances scored by Claude-3.7
- `evaluation_method` not `human-expert-eval` · [S1][writingbench-s1]
  - why: Five annotators judged pairs of responses, but on 300 queries outside the benchmark and to validate the judge; no published score comes from people.
  > Five professionally trained annotators with linguistic backgrounds perform pairwise comparisons of model responses.
- `designed_for_subjects` not `reasoning-model` · [S1][writingbench-s1]
  - why: Reasoning models are scored, with and without thinking, and their reasoning is stripped before grading; they are admitted, not the designed-for case.
  > For models capable of reasoning, the reasoning content is excluded from the evaluated response.

**Open review checks** (12):

1. (field `domain`) WritingBench was chosen for the empty creative-writing leaf over LitBench (2025, human preference pairs on Reddit stories) and EQ-Bench's Creative Writing v3. LitBench's scored act is judging which of two stories people preferred, which tests evaluators rather than writers, and its items carry Reddit users' stories; Creative Writing v3 has no paper and is run from an individual's project. WritingBench has a NeurIPS paper, open queries and rubrics, a repository, a board, an inspect\_evals task and 2026 use. Those comparisons rest on general knowledge, not on Sources read for this entry. No Epoch stub exists; the id writingbench is proposed.
2. (field `domain`) language/generation is primary and creative-writing secondary, with the Literature & Arts subset (183 of 1,000) overriding to creative-writing. A reviewer may prefer a separate entry for a purpose-built creative-writing benchmark so that the leaf has a primary entry of its own. · [S1][writingbench-s1]
   > Politics & Law 201 Literature & Arts 183 Education 111 Advertising & Marketing 128
3. (field `evaluation_method`) The grader changes by stage and by date. Criteria are Claude-3.7's, the paper's numbers are the critic model's (1-10), and the board's are Claude-3-7-Sonnet's, Claude-Sonnet-4's and now Claude-Sonnet-4-5's (0-100), none with a snapshot id. The README's Quick Start still recommends Claude-3-7-Sonnet. Whether the board rescored every model when the judge changed is not stated. · [S7][writingbench-s7]
   > Scored by: Claude-Sonnet-4-5
4. (field `versions`) The two judge switches are modelled as revisions although the queries did not change, so a claim can name the judge it was scored under; the 04 S4 rule is written for item changes. Whether the 1,000 queries of 2025-04-29 are a subset of the first 1,239 is not stated, so revision or edition for that step is a judgement. · [S5][writingbench-s5]
   > Switch to \*\*Claude-Sonnet-4\*\* for evaluation.
5. (field `governance.independence_flags`) grader-from-evaluated-party rests on Claude-Sonnet-4-5 judging a board on which it and other Anthropic models are scored; the same model family wrote the criteria and trained the critic. MUSE's judge (claude-sonnet-4-6) also scores Claude Sonnet 4.6 outputs. No Source measures self-preference on WritingBench. · [S3][writingbench-s3]
   > the judge is claude-sonnet-4-6
6. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type is null. The paper's front matter gives Alibaba Group, Renmin University of China and Shanghai Jiao Tong University as the authors' affiliations (not quoted, because the author names and e-mail addresses sit beside them). If X-PLUG is held by that company, maintainer\_type is industry-lab and maintainer-competes-on-own-benchmark extends to the board's Alibaba (Qwen) rows. · [S6][writingbench-s6]
   > qwen3-235b-a22b-thinking-2507,82.34,1000,Alibaba
7. (field `capability`) capability is context-integration alone. instruction-following was rejected because the source frames style, format and length as writing requirements graded by degree and does not claim instruction following; the category-specific (C) scores do isolate requirement criteria, which a reviewer may count. No capability term names writing quality itself (logged with bench tag-gap).
8. (field `data.data_provenance`) data\_provenance is model-generated. The materials were collected from public documents by annotators (web-scraped?), and experts revised every query and wrote some (expert-authored?); the sources do not say how many queries the experts wrote. 445 queries are Chinese; a reviewer who reads Chinese could confirm the language counts and the materials' provenance. · [S1][writingbench-s1]
   > Their role is to collect open-source reference materials needed for the writing tasks (e.g., public financial statements or legal templates).
9. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk medium. The evaluator-side routes (a critic trained on the benchmark's own queries and criteria; the maintainers' writing models trained on critic-selected data) are recorded in the note, not as contamination\_evidence, because neither puts the items into an entrant's training data. · [S1][writingbench-s1]
   > When building the training data of scoring prompts, the queries and criteria are drawn from WritingBench
10. (field `activity`) activity no-submission-channel, although the README invites contact by GitHub or e-mail about leaderboard construction; if the maintainers evaluate models on request, accepting-submissions with maintainer-run may fit better.

### 2.4 MT-Bench (mt-bench)

`data/benchmarks/language/mt-bench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*80 two-turn questions in eight categories, each turn graded 1 to 10 by a GPT-4 judge, from LMSYS's FastChat.*

A fixed set of 80 two-turn questions for chat assistants, 10 in each of eight categories: writing, roleplay, extraction, reasoning, math, coding, knowledge I (STEM) and knowledge II (humanities and social science). The second turn is a follow-up to the first, such as a rewrite under a new constraint. Answers are graded by GPT-4 acting as judge. The default, single-answer grading, scores each turn from 1 to 10 and reports the mean over all 160 turns; math, reasoning and coding are graded against reference answers that GPT-4 itself wrote, and the second-turn prompt shows the judge the whole conversation. Two pairwise modes report win rates instead, against gpt-3.5-turbo or between all pairs. The paper that introduced it studies the judge's biases (position, verbosity and self-enhancement, and weak grading of math and reasoning) and measures 85% agreement between GPT-4 and 58 expert labellers on non-tied votes, above the 81% the labellers reach among themselves. The questions, prompts, reference answers and code are in FastChat's llm\_judge package, and 3,355 expert votes are released on Hugging Face. OpenAI shut down gpt-4-0314, the judge snapshot of the paper's case studies, on 2026-03-26, and shuts down gpt-4-0613 and the gpt-4 alias, the harness's default judge, on 2026-10-23.

### 2.5 XL-Sum (xlsum)

`data/benchmarks/language/xlsum.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*BBC article-summary pairs in 44 languages (45 in v2.0), for multilingual abstractive summarization scored by ROUGE.*

A multilingual abstractive summarization dataset built from the BBC's news sites. Most BBC articles open with a bold paragraph of one or two sentences, written by the article's author, that sums up the story; XL-Sum takes that paragraph as the reference summary and the rest of the article as the input. The paper's release (v1.0) holds 1,005,292 pairs in 44 languages, BBC's 43 language services with Serbian counted once per script, more than two-thirds of them low-resource by the paper's measure. The newer release (v2.0), which the maintainers recommend, adds Traditional Chinese and holds about 1.35 million pairs, deduplicated and split 80/10/10 per language. Systems generate a summary of each test article in its language and are scored per language by ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-L against the BBC summary. Because ROUGE depends on tokenization and stemming, the repository ships a multilingual adaptation of Google's rouge-score with language-specific stemmers and word segmenters, and how a score was computed is part of what it means. The baselines are mT5 models fine-tuned on the training split; prompted LLMs are now scored on it too, in suites such as AfroBench.

| Classification | |

### 2.6 WMT General Machine Translation (wmt-general-mt)

`data/benchmarks/language/wmt-general-mt.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-11-18

*The Conference on Machine Translation's yearly general MT shared task, ranked by professional human evaluation.*

The main shared task of WMT, the Conference on Machine Translation (a workshop from 2006 to 2015, then a conference under ACL's SIGMT), formerly the News translation task. Each year the organisers build new test sets of recent, source-original documents, have professional agencies translate them, and release the sources as a blind set; teams translate them within about two weeks and upload the outputs to OCELoT, where no score is shown. The organisers also collect translations from popular LLMs and anonymised online services. The official ranking comes from human evaluation: Error Span Annotation (ESA) since 2024, with MQM for some pairs, by professional translators and, for some pairs, a paid crowd; systems are ranked by score into significance clusters per language pair. WMT25 had 30 language pairs, half human-evaluated, over news, social, speech, literary, education and dialogue documents. An automatic ranking (AutoRank: LLM judges and learned metrics, chrF++ for the lowest-resource pairs) chose which systems reached human evaluation and ranked the rest. WMT26 (23 pairs, instructions attached to each sample) evaluates every primary system by contrastive ESA and publishes no automatic ranking. Systems compete in a constrained track (open weights under 20B parameters) and an unconstrained one, and sources, outputs, references and judgements are released after each round.

#### wmt-general-mt · Identity and id

#### wmt-general-mt · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary language/translation; secondary language/low-resource-languages, language/multilingual; per_edition true · [S1][wmt-general-mt-s1]
  - why: Every edition scores translations of documents from a source language into a target language, one direction at a time.
  > Formerly known as News translation task of the WMT focusses on evaluation of general capabilities of machine translation (MT) systems.
- `capability` = generation-fidelity · [S2][wmt-general-mt-s2]
  - why: Raters mark error spans in each translation against its source and score it from 0 to 100 (ESA), or have error categories weighted into a score (MQM); the score is faithfulness to the source document. The taxonomy uses this benchmark's 2025 edition as the term's example.
  > \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\]
- `evaluation_method` = human-expert-eval, human-crowd-eval, model-graded-judge, model-derived-metric, reference-metric, entrant-relative-ranking · [S2][wmt-general-mt-s2]
  - why: The official result is human evaluation, ESA or MQM, by professional translators and linguists for most pairs and by a paid crowd screened on platform performance for others. Through WMT25 an automatic ranking chose which systems reached human evaluation and stayed the official result for the rest. It averaged robustly scaled scores from two GEMBA-ESA judges (GPT-4.1 and Command A, prompted LLMs) and three learned metrics (MetricX-24-Hybrid-XL, XCOMET-XL and CometKiwi-XL). For Bhojpuri and Maasai it used chrF++ alone, a fixed-formula reference metric. Ranks are ranges over Wilcoxon tests against the other systems, grouped into clusters, and AutoRank is rescaled from 1 to the number of systems, so both move with the pool.
  > Systems not selected for human evaluation keep their AUTORANK ranking as the official result for that language pair
- `designed_for_subjects` = task-specific-supervised-model, instruction-tuned-model, full-product-pipeline, human-expert · [S2][wmt-general-mt-s2]
  - why: The task was built for trained MT systems, and most 2025 entrants fine-tuned LLMs for translation. The organisers also prompt general LLMs zero-shot with each domain's instruction, add three online translation services as shipped products (ONLINE-B, G and W), and rank the professional human references among the systems.
  > In line with previous years, we included translations from three public MT services, anonymized as ONLINE-{B,G,W}.
- `secondary_axes` = cost · [S2][wmt-general-mt-s2]
  - why: The WMT25 findings report each organiser-collected LLM's token counts and estimated translation cost beside its rank.
  > The estimated costs shown are for the main test set and do not include the test suites.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `multimodal/video-language` · [S1][wmt-general-mt-s1]
  - why: The speech domain's sources are videos, and the human raters judge translations against the video, but systems receive an ASR transcript and may ignore the video; what is scored is the translation of one domain among four or more. The corpus classification logs the same gap (failure 2026-09-28-wmt25-general-mt-shared-task-001).
  > The speech domain is going to be released with the original video together with machine generated transcript.
- `capability` not `instruction-following` · [S3][wmt-general-mt-s3]
  - why: WMT26 attaches instructions to each sample (formality, glossaries, structured formats, style), but ignoring one is counted as a translation error inside the same ESA score, not scored apart from translation quality.
  > not following instructions will be considered a translation error
- `evaluation_method` not `composite` · [S3][wmt-general-mt-s3]
  - why: AutoRank averages a judge's and learned metrics' scores, but the headline is the human ESA or MQM score, one method; AutoRank selects systems and ranks only those not human-rated, and WMT26 dropped it.
  > All systems will be human evaluated - we will not rely on automatic evaluation to drop low performing systems

### 2.7 Belebele (belebele)

`data/benchmarks/language/belebele.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-09 · last verified 2026-11-09

*900 multiple-choice reading-comprehension questions on FLORES-200 passages, parallel across 122 language variants.*

A multiple-choice machine reading comprehension set from Meta AI, built so that models can be compared across many languages on the same items. Each of its 900 questions is tied to one of 488 short passages taken from FLORES-200's public dev and devtest splits, and has four candidate answers of which one is correct. The questions and answers were written in English by a language service provider's annotators over five feedback rounds, filtered by statistical checks for shortcut-solvable items, and then translated by fluent human translators, without machine translation, to pair with FLORES-200's existing translation of each passage. The result is fully parallel across 122 language variants (115 languages, 29 scripts, 27 families), including romanized Hindi, Urdu, Bengali, Nepali and Sinhala, which FLORES-200 lacks; 109,800 rows in all. The questions avoid multi-hop and commonsense reasoning and are meant to need only the passage, so the score is plain accuracy per language variant against a chance level of 25%. Belebele is a test set only; for models that need fine-tuning the maintainers assemble an English training set from six other multiple-choice datasets. The paper scores fine-tuned multilingual masked language models, five-shot base LLMs and zero-shot instruction-tuned models; four authors answering English questions blind averaged 97.6%.

#### belebele · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary language/multilingual; secondary language/understanding, language/low-resource-languages · [S3][belebele-s3]
  - why: The benchmark's purpose is to run one task, identically, in 122 language variants and compare models across them, which is the multilingual leaf's definition; the items are made parallel for that comparison. The task is reading comprehension with the answer determined by a supplied passage (understanding), and the set is built to reach low-resource languages that lacked any such benchmark (low-resource-languages).
  > Being fully parallel, this dataset enables direct comparison of model performance across all languages.
- `capability` = context-integration · [S3][belebele-s3]
  - why: Each question is answered from a supplied passage, and the questions were written so that the answer rests on what the passage states and cannot be had from knowledge a model already holds; the score is whether the model chose the option the passage supports.
  > MCQs enable us to better center the questions on information explicitly stated in the passage
- `evaluation_method` = multiple-choice · [S3][belebele-s3]
  - why: The system picks one of four supplied answers and is scored by accuracy; chance is 25%. The paper notes that for instruction-tuned models whose generated answer is matched to a letter the 25% floor does not strictly hold, since an unparseable reply scores nothing.
  > With 4 candidate answers for each question, the expected accuracy for sequence classification models that guess randomly is 0.25.
- `designed_for_subjects` = base-model, instruction-tuned-model, task-specific-supervised-model · [S3][belebele-s3]
  - why: The paper evaluates three kinds of entrant on the same items, masked language models fine-tuned on an English multiple-choice training set (or its machine translations), pretrained LLMs prompted five-shot and instruction-tuned models prompted zero-shot, and the README lists settings for each.
  > For LLMs, we evaluate several models using In-Context Learning and also instruction-tuned models via Zero-Shot.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `general-intelligence/multi-subject-knowledge-exams` · [S3][belebele-s3]
  - why: The 2026 audit files Belebele under QA / Knowledge, but the questions are built to need only the passage and no external knowledge, so breadth of knowledge is not what is scored.
  > answering does not require presumptions or external knowledge as is required in more difficult reasoning datasets
- `capability` not `knowledge-recall` · [S3][belebele-s3]
  - why: The passage is supplied and the questions are built not to need outside knowledge.
  > answering does not require presumptions or external knowledge as is required in more difficult reasoning datasets
- `capability` not `deductive-reasoning` · [S3][belebele-s3]
  - why: The authors deliberately exclude multi-hop and commonsense reasoning so that the score separates levels of language comprehension only.
  > we intentionally create questions that do not require higher levels of information processing, such as multi-hop or commonsense reasoning
- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S3][belebele-s3]
  - why: The paper scores masked language models fine-tuned on English data in every other language (zero-shot cross-lingual transfer), which moves only the input language. That is one evaluation setting among several, not the benchmark's design; its scores are per-language accuracies, not a shifted condition against an in-distribution one.
  > the parallel nature also enables a number of cross-lingual evaluation settings
- `evaluation_method` not `exact-match` · [S3][belebele-s3]
  - why: Zero-shot instructed models reply with a letter that is post-processed and matched, but the reply still selects among the four supplied options, which is multiple choice.
  > We post-process answers and accept multiple formats.

**Open review checks** (10):

1. (field `domain`) Primary is multilingual, with understanding and low-resource-languages secondary. The family's other entries put the task first (flores translation, xlsum summarization, squad understanding); Belebele is the case for multilingual-first, since the items exist to be compared across languages, but understanding could be argued primary for consistency.
2. (field `lineage.role`) lineage.role is fork, from FLORES-200. Meta AI built FLORES-200 and Belebele, so at release the maintainer was the same (variant); FLORES is now OLDI's FLORES+. It could also be role root, since the task is new and only the passages are shared. flores.yaml's lineage.forks (or variants) could list belebele.
3. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk medium. The evidence read concerns the FLORES passages (BLOOMZ's FLORES fine-tuning; an audit's FLORES findings, which disagree by method), not Belebele's question-answer pairs, which no source read tests; whether FLORES evidence should count for Belebele, and whether high is warranted, is open. · [S6][belebele-s6]
   > prior surface-form methods flag 7 of 7 models, yet STAMP detects contamination in only 1.2% of model
4. (field `governance.independence_flags`) The paper's LLM baselines include the LLaMA 1 and LLaMA 2 families; whether they come from the maintainer's own organisation is not stated in the sources read, so no independence flag is set. There is no board to compete on.
5. (field `data.ceiling_anchor_type`) ceiling\_anchor\_type is crowd-average from four authors answering about 120 English questions; it says nothing about the other 121 variants, and authors are not a crowd sample.
6. (field `execution.harness_availability`) harness\_availability reference-implementation-only. The paper says its answer post-processing code is in the repository, but the repository holds only the training-set script and sample instructions; lm-evaluation-harness's group is not designated by the maintainers. none could be argued. · [S3][belebele-s3]
   > Code provided at github.com/facebookresearch/belebele
7. (field `versions`) No versions are recorded. The commit histories of the repository and the Hugging Face dataset (read through their APIs, not quoted Sources) show no change to the items after the 2023 upload; the paper's errata on FLORES translations were handled inside Belebele, not as a release. Whether the direct-download archive and the Hugging Face copy are identical was not checked.
8. (field `lineage`) The variant and fork ids (2m-belebele, belebele-extractive-qa) are proposed, not allocated. The fork's maintainers' affiliations were not read; the 2M-Belebele paper was read only as its abstract, and whether its ASL part was released was not established.
9. (field `designed_for_subjects`) designed\_for\_subjects includes task-specific-supervised-model for the fine-tuned masked language models, although Belebele itself is test-only; the fine-tuning uses the assembled training set from other datasets. · [S1][belebele-s1]
   > The Belebele dataset is intended to be used only as a test set, and not for training or validation.
10. (field `aggregation_policy`) aggregation\_policy official-aggregate rests on the paper's summary averages over the 122 variants; the README defines only per-setting accuracy, and later papers report chosen variants, so none-by-design or community-aggregate could be argued.

**Evidence** (40 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### ruler · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][ruler-s1]
  > we create a new synthetic benchmark RULER with flexible configurations for customized sequence length and task complexity
- `released` = 2024-04-09 · [S2][ruler-s2]
  > Submitted on 9 Apr 2024
- `release_venue` = COLM 2024 · [S2][ruler-s2]
  > COLM 2024; Code is available at

#### ruler · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary language/long-context · [S1][ruler-s1]
  - why: The benchmark's subject is how well a language model uses a long input, and its difficulty is set by the input's length; every task is run at increasing lengths to find where performance drops.
  > In this work, we propose RULER, a new benchmark to evaluate long-context modeling capabilities for language models
- `capability` = context-integration · [S1][ruler-s1]
  - why: Every answer is fixed by material the input supplies, such as random values hidden in a haystack, a chain of variable bindings, word counts in a synthetic list or a gold paragraph among distractors. The inputs are synthetic so that knowledge the model already holds does not help.
  > The synthetic input in RULER reduces reliance on parametric knowledge, which interferes with the utilization of long-context input in realistic tasks
- `evaluation_method` = reference-metric · [S1][ruler-s1]
  - why: Each task scores the share of the reference strings (the inserted values, the variable names, the top words) found case-insensitively in the output, a fixed-formula recall against references with partial credit when several strings are expected. For QA one of the reference answers is enough. The headline averages these per-task accuracies.
  > we append the task input with an answer prefix and check the presence of the target output with recall-based accuracy
- `designed_for_subjects` = instruction-tuned-model, base-model · [S1][ruler-s1]
  - why: The main results are aligned models prompted through their chat templates with an answer prefix appended. Base models are run by plain continuation of the same prompt and answer prefix, with their own Llama2-7B (base) threshold in Appendix F.
  > Our results in the main text only include aligned models (GPT-4, Gemini-1.5, and 15 open-source models). Besides the aligned models, we also evaluate 7 open-source base models using RULER.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `language/retrieval-qa` · [S1][ruler-s1]
  - why: The QA category's gold paragraphs are inside the input, among distractor paragraphs; the system retrieves nothing from a corpus first, which the leaf's definition asks.
  > In this task category, we insert the golden paragraphs (i.e., the paragraphs that contain answers) into paragraphs randomly sampled from the same dataset.
- `domain` not `reasoning-general/logical-deduction` · [S1][ruler-s1]
  - why: Variable tracking is decidable from the stated bindings, but it is one task of 13, the paper frames it as a proxy for coreference resolution, and the object of study is long-context modelling, not a reasoning form (reasoning-general's inclusion test).
  > Multi-hop Tracing: we propose variable tracking, a minimal proxy task for coreference chain resolution to check the behavior of tracing entities with multi-hop connections.
- `capability` not `memory-retention` · [S1][ruler-s1]
  - why: The needle sits earlier in the input than the query at its end, but the whole input is in the window when the query is read. The term's exclusion keeps it off benchmarks where only the input is long, and RULER does not vary or report the distance between needle and query.
  > Current RULER reports a single number metric for each input length without providing the depth-level performance.
- `evaluation_method` not `exact-match` · S3
  - why: The output is not compared for equality with the reference. A reference string counts if it appears anywhere in the output, and multi-answer tasks give partial credit, which the term's exclusion test rules out.
  > score = sum(\[sum(\[1.0 if r.lower() in pred.lower() else 0.0 for r in ref\]) / len(ref) for pred, ref in zip(preds, refs)\]) / len(preds) \* 100

#### ruler · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system Gemini-1.5-Pro · [S1][ruler-s1]

- `task` = exists true; input a generated text of the target length in the model's own tokens (distractor essays, noise sentences, synthetic word lists or distractor paragraphs) with the task's key information inserted, followed by the question and an answer prefix; output A short answer, such as the requested values, the variable names bound to a value, the most common or most frequent words, or the answer to the question.; scoring Per task, the share of reference strings found in the output (any one answer for QA), averaged over 500 samples per length; the 13 task scores are averaged at each length. A model's effective length is the longest tested length whose average beats Llama2-7B (chat) at 4K (85.6%). Two weighted averages over the lengths, one weighting long inputs more (inc) and one short inputs (dec), rank the models.; metric_range 0, 100 · [S1][ruler-s1]

**Open review checks** (8):

1. (field `evaluation_method`) evaluation\_method is reference-metric, a fixed-formula recall of reference strings found anywhere in the output with partial credit. exact-match was rejected because the output need not equal the reference, though Mellum 2 calls the scorer exact-match and many readers would file it there. · S3
   > score = sum(\[max(\[1.0 if r.lower() in pred.lower() else 0.0 for r in ref\]) for pred, ref in zip(preds, refs)\]) / len(preds) \* 100
2. (field `comparability.material_extra`) The input length is carried in context\_window\_used, read as the length a run was scored at. If that field means the model's configured window instead, the length belongs in subset\_used (for example "13 tasks at 131072 tokens"), and a new length field may be needed. Lengths are counted in each model's own tokenizer, so "128K" is not the same text across models.
3. (field `execution.runnable_via`) lm-evaluation-harness's QA scorer gives the share of reference answers found, where RULER's own counts a sample right if any one answer appears, so lm-eval scores QA samples with several distinct answers lower. Confirm before treating lm-eval RULER numbers as comparable. · [S7][ruler-s7]
   > score = max( sum(1.0 if r.lower() in pred.lower() else 0.0 for r in ref) / len(ref)

   > branch to use our latest pipeline for RULERv2 evaluation

6. (field `capability`) memory-retention was rejected as the input is all in the window and needle depth is not reported; the needle does precede the query by the whole haystack, which the term's inclusion test describes.
7. (field `data.data_provenance`) data\_provenance is synthetic-procedural only. The haystack essays (from the web) and the SQuAD and HotpotQA questions are re-used text whose provenance the sources read do not state; web-scraped or crowd-authored could be added from those datasets' own papers. · S5

### 2.9 HotpotQA (hotpotqa)

`data/benchmarks/language/hotpotqa.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*113k crowd-written Wikipedia questions that need two paragraphs to answer, scored on answers and supporting sentences.*

A multi-hop question answering dataset over English Wikipedia: 112,779 questions written by crowd workers, each shown two linked Wikipedia paragraphs and asked for a question that needs both. Most are bridge questions, answered through an intermediate entity; the rest compare two entities, some as yes/no questions. Workers also marked the sentences that support each answer, so a system returns an answer and its supporting facts. There are two settings, each with its own test set of 7,405 questions whose answers are withheld. In the distractor setting the two gold paragraphs are shuffled with eight retrieved by bigram tf-idf; in the fullwiki setting the system must find the evidence among the first paragraphs of all of Wikipedia. Answers are scored by exact match and token F1, supporting facts by exact match and F1 against the annotated set, and joint metrics combine the two. Training and dev sets are public. Test scores came from CodaLab, where distractor entrants submitted code in a Docker environment and fullwiki entrants submitted prediction files; the two leaderboards' newest rows are from 2023 and 2024. A September 2026 multi-hop retrieval paper still reports answer EM and F1 on it, with its own retrieval and reader.

#### hotpotqa · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary language/retrieval-qa; secondary language/understanding · [S1][hotpotqa-s1]
  - why: The fullwiki setting gives the system only the question and the whole of Wikipedia's first paragraphs, so the evidence must be retrieved first, the retrieval-qa leaf's case; the paper calls it the setting that truly tests multi-hop reasoning, and current use retrieves from a corpus too. The distractor setting supplies ten paragraphs that determine the answer, the understanding leaf's case, and carries that leaf as its domain\_override in subsets\[\].
  > This full wiki setting truly tests the performance of the systems
- `capability` = context-integration · [S1][hotpotqa-s1]
  - why: The answer is determined by supplied material, ten paragraphs in the distractor setting or the released Wikipedia corpus in the fullwiki one, and the score checks both the answer and which supplied sentences the system used.
  > Most of the questions require at least one supporting fact from each paragraph to answer.
- `evaluation_method` = exact-match, reference-metric, classification-metric, composite · [S1][hotpotqa-s1]
  - why: Six numbers per entry. Answer EM is exact match after normalisation; answer F1 is token overlap with the reference answer, a fixed-formula reference metric. Supporting-fact EM and F1 compare the predicted set of (title, sentence) pairs with the gold set, F1 being a classification statistic over each question's sentences. Joint EM and F1 multiply the answer's and the supporting facts' precision and recall, combining sub-scores of different methods; the leaderboards are ordered by joint F1.
  > The second set features joint metrics that combine the evaluation of answer spans and supporting facts as follows.
- `designed_for_subjects` = task-specific-supervised-model, retrieval-augmented-system · [S4][hotpotqa-s4]
  - why: The entrants the paper and leaderboards were built for are QA models trained on HotpotQA's own training set and scored as trained. In the fullwiki setting the entrant's own retrieval is inside the scored system, which the README encourages in place of the released tf-idf paragraphs.
  > If you want to use your own IR system (which is encouraged!)

Considered and rejected:

- `capability` not `deductive-reasoning` · [S1][hotpotqa-s1]
  - why: Bridge and comparison questions chain facts across two paragraphs, but correctness is equality or overlap with a crowd-written answer, not decidability from premises, and the authors judge about 6% of sampled questions single-hop and 2% unanswerable.
  > about 6% of the sampled questions can be answered with one of the two paragraphs, and 2% of them unanswerable
- `capability` not `quantitative-reasoning` · [S1][hotpotqa-s1]
  - why: Some comparison questions need arithmetic, such as counting or comparing dates, but the scored answer is mostly an entity, and no number is required as such.
  > sometimes require arithmetic such as counting

**Open review checks** (8):

1. (field `domain`) Primary domain is retrieval-qa (fullwiki) with the distractor setting as an understanding subset. The distractor board is the one the paper and site list first, and its test set is the more protected, so the primary could be swapped. · [S1][hotpotqa-s1]
   > This full wiki setting truly tests the performance of the systems
2. (field `activity`) activity is unknown because the CodaLab Worksheets guide could not be read (expired TLS certificate, 2026-10-07). If CodaLab still scores HotpotQA submissions this is accepting-submissions; if it has stopped, closed. · [S6][hotpotqa-s6]
   > To submit your models and evaluate them on the official test sets, please read our submission guide hosted on Codalab.
3. (field `evaluation_method`) evaluation\_method has four terms: classification-metric for supporting-fact F1 (a per-question sentence-set F1, averaged) and composite for the joint metrics. A lighter reading takes both F1s as one overlap measure (reference-metric), which would rule composite out. Answer EM also strips punctuation and articles (hotpot\_evaluate\_v1.py, read but not cited), a little beyond exact-match's whitespace-or-case normalisation. · [S1][hotpotqa-s1]
   > The second set features joint metrics that combine the evaluation of answer spans and supporting facts as follows.
4. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type community-collective follows the shared hotpotqa organisation account; academic-lab fits if the CMU host of the data files is taken as the holder.
5. (field `governance.independence_flags`) funded-by-evaluated-party rests on a 2018 Facebook ParlAI Research Award and on later Facebook AI rows on the boards; maintainer-competes rests on IRRR by two of the authors. · [S1][hotpotqa-s1]
   > This work is partly funded by the Facebook ParlAI Research Award.
6. (field `data.access`) data.access is train-open-test-held-out after the fullwiki setting; the distractor setting alone would be private-test-server, and subsets cannot carry their own access.
7. (field `data.refresh`) refresh static treats the v1.1 training file (extremely short questions removed, 2018-11-06) as outside the scored content; versioned-releases fits if a training-set revision counts.
8. (field `comparability`) The (composite, retrieval-augmented-system) pair resolves to the agentic profile, which makes scaffold, sandbox and harness material; for a QA dataset the retrieval corpus and reader model matter more, which the profile has no fields for.

### 2.10 MasakhaNER (masakhaner)

`data/benchmarks/language/masakhaner.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-09 · last verified 2026-11-09

*Named-entity recognition on human-annotated local news in 21 African languages, scored by entity-level F1.*

A named-entity recognition benchmark for African languages built by the Masakhane community. Sentences of local news text are annotated by native speakers with four entity types, personal names (PER), locations (LOC), organizations (ORG) and dates and times (DATE), in CoNLL format with train, development and test splits per language. MasakhaNER 1.0 (TACL 2021) covers ten languages from West and East Africa, with volunteer annotators; MasakhaNER 2.0 (EMNLP 2022) covers twenty, adding Southern and Central African languages, newly annotated with paid annotators and language coordinators and drawn partly from the MAFAND-MT translation corpus. It keeps nine of 1.0's languages, on new text with its own test sets, and drops Amharic. Systems tag each test sentence and are scored per language by micro-averaged entity-level F1. The papers' baselines are multilingual encoders fine-tuned per language, and the 2.0 paper studies zero-shot transfer from other source languages. Prompted LLMs are now scored on MasakhaNER-X, the repository's aggregation of both editions for XTREME-UP, which recasts the task as generating the entities as text; in AfroBench (2025) they trail a fine-tuned AfroXLMR baseline by about 34 to 44 F1 points.

#### masakhaner · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary language/information-extraction; secondary language/low-resource-languages, language/multilingual · [S2][masakhaner-s2]
  - why: The scored act is finding the named entities in a sentence and labelling each span with its type, extracting structured records (entities) from unstructured text, the information-extraction leaf's definition; the 2.0 paper chose NER for that use. Both papers build the data because African languages lack annotated datasets, which is the low-resource leaf, and the same task is scored and compared per language across ten and twenty languages, which is the multilingual leaf.
  > because of its utility in downstream applications such as question answering and information extraction
- `capability` = context-integration · [S2][masakhaner-s2]
  - why: The sentence supplied is the material that determines the answer, the entity spans and their types, and the score checks whether the system marked them correctly; both papers report separately on test entities never seen in training, which a system can only find from the sentence itself.
  > zero-frequency entities that do not appear in the training corpus
- `evaluation_method` = classification-metric · [S2][masakhaner-s2]
  - why: F1 is a statistic of the whole set of predicted against annotated entities, the term's named case.
  > For evaluation, we make use of the microaveraged F1 score.
- `designed_for_subjects` = task-specific-supervised-model · [S2][masakhaner-s2]
  - why: Both papers' baselines are pretrained encoders (mBERT, XLM-R, AfroXLM-R and others) fine-tuned on each language's training split and scored as trained artifacts.
  > evaluate performance on the test set using HuggingFace Transformers

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `language/translation` · [S2][masakhaner-s2]
  - why: Nothing is translated. 2.0 annotates some MAFAND-MT translations as source text, but the task is tagging them in their own language.
  > which consists of French and English news articles translated into 11 languages
- `capability` not `transfer-learning` · [S2][masakhaner-s2]
  - why: The 2.0 paper's experiments are cross-lingual transfer from other source languages, but that is a protocol the paper studies; the benchmark scores in-language tagging on each test split, whatever the system was trained on (see review\_checks).
  > choosing the best transfer language improves zero-shot F1 scores by an average of 14 points across 20 languages compared to using English

**Open review checks** (11):

1. (field `versions`) One family with two editions, by 04 S4 (same maintainer and repository, same task and tag set, new items). The editions have separate papers, separate Hugging Face datasets and separate citation instructions, which the rule's "independently versioned and cited" could read as two benchmarks. · [S5][masakhaner-s5]
   > If you make use of the MasakhaNER 1.0 dataset, please cite the our TACL paper.
2. (field `versions`) The README says 2.0 "includes all MasakhaNER 1.0, except for Amharic", while the 2.0 paper describes new news sources and separate test sets for the shared languages. Read as "all 1.0 languages"; whether any 1.0 sentences were carried into 2.0 was not established. · [S5][masakhaner-s5]
   > An expansion of MasakhaNER 1.0 to 20 African languages, the dataset includes all MasakhaNER 1.0, except for Amharic
3. (field `data.size`) The 2.0 README's split table gives Mossi 1,613 and Naija 1,294 test sentences, the reverse of the paper's Table 1 (1,294 and 1,613); Bambara and Setswana training counts also differ by one and 200. Which matches the released files was not checked. · [S7][masakhaner-s7]
   > 4532 \| 648 \| 1613 \|
4. (field `data.dataset_licence`) Licence disagreement. The README says CC BY-NC 4.0 for the NER data; Hugging Face's masakhaner2 record says afl-3.0 and masakhaner's says unknown. CC-BY-NC-4.0 was recorded from the maintainers' README. · [S4][masakhaner-s4]
   > "license:afl-3.0"
5. (field `data.dataset_licence`) The 1.0 Hugging Face record (masakhane/masakhaner) states no licence; whether its files match the GitHub data folder was not checked. · [S8][masakhaner-s8]
   > "license:unknown"
6. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type community-collective rests on no legal form being stated for Masakhane in the sources read; nonprofit if a registered Masakhane body holds the repository and datasets. 1.0's annotators volunteered through the community. · [S9][masakhaner-s9]
   > volunteered through the Masakhane community
7. (field `governance.independence_flags`) Lacuna Fund, 2.0's funder, is co-founded by Google.org among others, and AfroBench scores models whose developers were not checked against that; funded-by-evaluated-party was not set on outside knowledge. · [S2][masakhaner-s2]
   > This work was carried out with support from Lacuna Fund, an initiative co-founded by The Rockefeller Foundation, Google.org, and
8. (field `lineage`) MasakhaNER-X as a same-maintainer variant. It sits in the Masakhane repository but was built for XTREME-UP and is cited in AfroBench to the XTREME-UP paper; a fork (another maintainer) is arguable. AfroBench's per-language sizes (Amharic 500, Luo 185) are 1.0's test splits, though the README says MasakhaNER-X covers 20 languages. · [S3][masakhaner-s3]
   > excl. amh: 500 & luo: 185 (in MasakhaNER-X)
9. (field `capability`) Capability context-integration, with transfer-learning rejected. The 2.0 paper is about cross-lingual transfer and its headline result is zero-shot; transfer-learning is arguable as a second capability. NER has no capability term of its own (span labelling as a language competence).
10. (field `data.data_provenance`) data\_provenance expert-authored for native-speaker annotators trained on the MUC-6 guide; 1.0's annotators were unpaid volunteers who are its authors. crowd-authored is arguable. · [S2][masakhaner-s2]
   > The annotation was carried out by three native speakers per language recruited from AI/NLP communities in Africa.
11. (field `execution.harness_availability`) harness\_availability reference-implementation-only, not official-harness. The repository's code produced the papers' scores, but the maintainers do not designate it as the scorer for others' results.

**Reviewer checklist** for `masakhaner`:

- [ ] Identity and id: the name, aliases, id, paper and release date are right, and this is one benchmark, not a family or an edition of another
- [ ] Domain and capabilities: the primary and secondary subdomains, capabilities, evaluation methods and intended subjects fit, and no rejected term should have been kept
- [ ] Task and evaluation: the task, scoring, ground truth, entrants and harness read as the sources describe them
- [ ] Data and licence: access, refresh, provenance, sizes, subsets, contamination and licences match the sources
- [ ] Governance and independence: maintainer type, submission process, funding and independence flags are right
- [ ] Lifecycle and activity: lifecycle, activity, versions, editions and history are current
- [ ] Every open review check above is answered or resolved
- [ ] Nothing here would embarrass the catalogue in front of a specialist
